1:
Where this stands in the week has to be reconstructed, because Luke does not say. Augustine points out that he leaves out the return to Bethany, the fig-tree and the answer about faith, and does not follow the days in order; the vague opening refers to the day the other two name. Gill counts it out — the entry, the night at Bethany, the cursing of the fig-tree and the clearing of the temple, the withered tree found on the return — so the deputation meets Jesus in the temple on the second morning after. Robertson and Clarke both land on the Tuesday of passion week, the last day of teaching there.

Who came is worth pinning down, and Lightfoot does it from the Sanhedrin's composition. It was made up of priests, Levites and Israelites; so the scribes here are likely the Levites or the lower priests, and the elders the laymen not of the priestly tribe — men like Gamaliel, then president. Robertson reads the delegation politically — chief priests for the Sadducees, scribes for the Pharisees, a formal embassy from the council — and notes that the verb is an ingressive aorist meaning they stood up against him, suddenly.

Henry hears the same in the word. They meant to surprise him, hoping to catch him without an answer, and to frighten him, coming in a body and with violence — though how should he fear a wrath it lay in his own power to restrain? What they interrupted matters as much as what they said: Christ was preaching his own gospel, having not only purchased the salvation but published it, which puts an honour on preachers and on plain preaching to common people.

What the question means depends on who is asking. Eusebius supplies the grievance underneath it: by the law of Moses only the line of Levi had authority to teach and charge of the sacred buildings, so a man of Judah is a usurper — to which he answers that had they known the scriptures they would have recognised a priest after the order of Melchisedec. Bede takes the challenge as darker. To ask by whose authority is to doubt whether the power is God's at all, and to want it understood that it is the devil's; to think he works by another's power is plainly to deny that he is the Son of God. Gill notes what stung most: the clearing of the temple had cost the rulers their rents.

The counter-question is not evasion. Bede observes that a plain answer would have refuted the calumny, but a question makes them condemn themselves out of their own mouths, by speech or by silence. Theophylact reads it as an exposure of a settled habit — they had always resisted the Spirit, having refused Isaiah whom they had forgotten and John whom they had lately seen. Eusebius narrows what is actually asked: not where John came from, but where he got his baptism. Gill puts the implied argument plainly — whoever authorised John baptizing authorised Jesus preaching.

Their calculation is preserved in the text. Robertson notes that the verb for their reasoning means to cast up accounts together and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, while Luke's word for what the crowd would do means to throw stones down on them. Ellicott marks the escalation — where the other Gospels have a general fear of the people, Luke has stoning outright, which the city's treatment of Jesus and of Stephen shows to be no exaggeration. Gill says flatly that their answer was an untruth: they preferred to sacrifice conscience rather than interest. Henry concludes that those who bury the knowledge they have are justly denied more, and Bede gives the principle generally: truth is rightly withheld from a questioner who cannot understand it, or who from hatred does not deserve an answer.
9:
Who the parable is aimed at is settled by Luke's own wording. Augustine notes that Matthew abbreviated what Luke keeps — this was spoken not only to the rulers who had asked about authority but to the people as well; Gill takes it as addressed to both, Christ turning to the crowd after silencing the council though his principal view was still the priests. Eusebius says what it is for: a figure of what they were about to do to him, and of the rejection waiting for them.

The vineyard is not in doubt. Ambrose points to Isaiah, who identifies the vineyard of the Lord of Sabaoth as the house of Israel, and asks who else can have planted it. Eusebius marks the one difference between the two parables and it is the whole point of this one: Isaiah's denounces the vineyard, while this is directed not at the vineyard but at the men who farm it — the elders, the chief priests, the doctors, the nobles. Theophylact offers a reading that brings it home to the hearer: each of the people is the vineyard and each is also the husbandman, since every one of us has himself to look after.

The absence of the owner is read theologically rather than geographically. Theophylact denies that the Lord travels at all, being everywhere present; what the journey means is that he is more present to those who love him and withdraws from those who disregard him, and that he left them to the guidance of their own judgment. Cyril dates the withdrawal from Sinai, after which the visible presence was not given again — though no interval passed in which prophets and righteous men were not sent. Theophylact adds the reason for the long delay: an early demand would have looked impatient, and indulgence leaves obstinacy less excusable.

The servants are identified in sequence. Bede makes the first Moses, seeking for forty years the fruit of the law he had given; the second David, sent to stir the husbandmen by the music of his psalmody, and answered with what portion have we in David; the third the whole company of the prophets, of whom there is hardly one they did not persecute. He notes that the three orders together answer to what the risen Lord called the law of Moses, the prophets and the psalms. Theophylact reads the modest demand exactly: not the whole fruit but a part — for what does God gain from us except his own knowledge, which is our profit anyway. Chrysostom explains the ordering itself as mercy. God does not press all things at once but accommodates himself to men; if they despised the Son who came after the servants, they would have heard him even less had he come first.
13:
Then the owner deliberates, and the hesitation is the crux. Theophylact and Cyril both deny it springs from ignorance. The Lord speaks doubtfully so that human freedom may be preserved, and because the Son ought to have been reverenced — the doubtful form of words exists precisely so that nobody may plead that the divine presence made their refusal inevitable. Cyril's version is that every device of human help having been tried on a people no whit healed, something greater is added. Henry marks what that greater thing was by the change of voice: the prophets had spoken as servants, saying thus saith the Lord, while the Son speaks among his own as a son, verily I say unto you.

Even the killing is placed carefully. Bede insists the rulers crucified the Son not from ignorance but from envy, since they knew whose inheritance the heathen had been promised to be, and reads the casting out of the vineyard as the suffering outside the gate. Theophylact takes the same phrase differently: the people did not put him to death with their own hands but delivered him to Pilate and the Gentiles — or, on another reading, the vineyard is the scripture, and it was outside that they slew him. Henry hears the calculation in their speech, that killing the servants only brought more servants, but killing the son would leave nobody to send and the possession quiet at last.

The crowd's answer differs across the Gospels, and two solutions are offered. Theophylact has them pronounce the sentence first and then, catching the parable's drift, recoil with God forbid. Augustine divides the crowd instead: some had asked craftily and others had cried Blessed is he that cometh, so one part gave the true verdict and the other protested once they saw it was against themselves. Basil describes the position they were in — condemned men with nothing to say against plain justice — and adds what he takes to be the mercy of the whole procedure: God does not punish in secret but announces the sentence beforehand, so that it may still recall men to repentance. Ambrose reads the coming of the lord of the vineyard as the coming of the Son, in whom the Father's majesty is present.

Bede turns the whole parable inward before leaving it. A vineyard is let out to every one of the faithful, the mystery of baptism being entrusted to him to work; the first servant and the second and the third are sent whenever the Law and the Psalms and the Prophets are read; the servant is beaten when the word heard is despised or blasphemed; and the heir is killed, so far as one man can kill him, by whoever tramples the Son of God under foot by sin.
17:
Before the quotation there is a look, and three witnesses stop over it. Robertson notes that the participle is Luke's own, absent from Mark and Matthew, and calls the glance piercing; Ellicott says the verb means a gaze turned and fixed on its object; Wesley thinks it meant to sharpen attention. Gill hears the look speaking on its own account — that so it would indeed be, and they would reject the Messiah and bring ruin on themselves and their posterity.

The stone is then explained from both ends. Eusebius accounts for the metaphor by the incarnation: he is called a stone because of an earthly body cut out without hands, as in Daniel's vision, being born of the Virgin; and the stone is neither silver nor gold because he came as no glorious king but a man lowly and despised — which is why the builders rejected him. Theophylact dates the rejection to a sentence of theirs, that this man is not of God. Bede reads the corner as a question: how else is the prophecy to be fulfilled, except that Christ, rejected and killed by them, is preached to the Gentiles who will believe? Cyril makes the geometry explicit — a corner is where two walls meet, and scripture uses it of Jew and Gentile brought into one faith, the Saviour compacting both into one new man.

The two fates in the next verse are read as two distinct judgments. Cyril distinguishes them by object: falling on the stone is what happened to their souls when they were offended at Christ, while the stone falling on them is the captivity and the scattering — the people winnowed through the world like straw off a threshing floor. He asks that the order be marked: the wickedness first, the just vengeance after. Bede's division is by degree and leaves room for recovery: a sinner who nevertheless believes falls on the stone and is shaken, and is preserved through penitence; those who merely despise are shaken so that they cannot walk upright; but the man on whom it comes down is ground so fine that not a shard is left in which to drink a little water.

Gill guards the first clause against misuse, since falling on Christ can be said in a good sense: those meant are not the men who build on him by faith but those who stumble at him and fall through unbelief. The language is unusual, and both Robertson and Ellicott say so — the verb for being broken means to shatter and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, the verb for the grinding means first to winnow and then to reduce to powder, and the whole verse, absent from many of the best manuscripts in Matthew, stands in every manuscript of Luke.

The parable lands, and the reaction proves it. Robertson notes Luke's time-marker — in that very hour — as a sign that the council was angry enough to force the crisis at once, and sums up their reading of the parable in a phrase: the cap fitted them and they saw it. Cyril observes what they did with the warning: instead of departing from evil they gathered a fresh occasion for crime, and what checked them was not the commandment against slaying the innocent but the fear of the crowd — the fear of man set before the reverence of God. Bede sees them proving the parable true in the act of resenting it — they are the husbandmen, seeking to kill the heir whose unjust death the story said would be punished — and adds that the same is done daily by the man who is a brother in name only, restrained from breaking a unity he detests merely by the number of good people around him. Since they could not seize him themselves, they set about it through the governor.
20:
The trap is described more fully by Luke than by anyone else, and the witnesses take the extra detail seriously. Robertson explains the vocabulary: the verb for watching means watching from the side, insidiously; the noun for the men employed means people let down secretly into place, hired liers-in-wait, and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; and the stated goal, to hand him over to the governor, is Luke's alone. Clarke traces the same word to a root meaning to set in ambush, cites Hesychius on it and Josephus using it of a man bribed for a purpose, and concludes that these were men of the basest principles doing for hire what the Pharisees could not do themselves.

What they pretended to be is the part Henry will not pass over. They were to feign themselves just men, which he calls no new thing — the devil can transform himself into an angel of light, and a Pharisee can appear in the garb and speak the language of a disciple. Wesley glosses the pretence exactly as men of tender conscience, and Robertson quotes Plummer to the same effect, that they posed as scrupulous persons with a difficulty about their duty. Henry draws the practical warning from it, that ministers must be on their guard against some who feign themselves just, and be wise as serpents when in the midst of a generation of vipers.

Henry also names the strategy behind the whole manoeuvre. The council could not put him to death by law and would not risk a tumult, so having failed to be his judges they were content to be his prosecutors, provided they could incense the governor. He calls that the common artifice of persecuting church-rulers, to make the secular power the tool of their malice — Pilate would have let Christ live quietly enough had the chief priests not presented him.

The flattery is transparent and the question is not. Robertson notes that the compliments are part of the scheme, these students of the Pharisees openly endorsing the teaching they mean to destroy, and explains the Hebraism about accepting no man's person as taking the face at face value; Ellicott finds the same phrase again in Galatians. Gill locates the whole weight of the question in two words Luke alone supplies: nobody doubted whether the Romans might lawfully tax, the pretended difficulty was whether we — Abraham's seed, who boasted they were never in bondage — might pay an heathen emperor. Bede sets out the fork. Some held that tribute was owed for the security the Romans provided; the Pharisees held that a people who paid tithes and firstfruits could not be subject to human law. Say yes and the crowd would hear a man putting the nation under the yoke; say no and the guards standing by would arrest him as the leader of a sedition.
23:
The answer turns on a coin. Cyril insists that the question about the image is not ignorance — Jesus knew perfectly whose head was on the money, and asked so that their own answer might frame his; and he adds that the Caesar meant is Tiberius, all the Roman emperors bearing the name from the first Caius. Theophylact fastens on the verb: he did not say give but render, because it is a debt — your prince keeps your life quiet and defends you from enemies, and the very coin you are holding is his. Then he turns the same word round: God has given you understanding and reason, and those are to be rendered too, that you may not be reckoned among the beasts. Titus of Bostra puts the whole reply in a sentence, that God asks not money but faith. Bede specifies what the second half claims — tithes, firstfruits, offerings and sacrifices — while Henry distinguishes the two spheres, submitting in civil things to the civil power and reserving worship to God alone, since it is God only who has authority to say my son, give me thy heart.

Origen finds a further sense in the two images. Man carries one image received from God at his making and another contracted from the enemy through disobedience, as a man who does the works of darkness bears the likeness of the power whose works he does — so that rendering to Caesar means casting away the earthly image in order to render to God the heavenly one, which is to love him. Ambrose draws a plainer moral: do not covet the world's goods if you would not owe Caesar, for no one can be the Lord's who has not first renounced the world, and the contract of faith binds harder than the contract of money.

Their defeat is recorded with some relish. Robertson notes that the word means they did not have the strength for it, and that these star pupils went back silent, having failed to build any case at all; Ellicott hears an echo he calls undesigned, of the boy in the temple at whose answers the doctors were astonished, the childhood proving a prophecy of the manhood. Wesley adds the limit on the failure: they could not take hold of his words before the people — later, before the council and without the crowd, they would manage it.
27:
A second party takes the field, and Bede sets the two side by side. There were two heresies among the Jews: the Pharisees, who gloried in the righteousness of their traditions and were popularly called the separated, and the Sadducees, whose very name meant righteous and claimed for them what they were not. When the first went away defeated, the second came. Gill notes that it was the same day, the tribute question having just been put by the others.

What they denied was more than one article. Origen states it precisely: the sect denied not only the resurrection of the dead but held that the soul dies with the body — and they chose their moment, coming forward when they saw him teaching his disciples about the resurrection. Henry presses the same point into its consequences. To say there is no resurrection is to say there is no return of the body to life, no continuance of the soul, no world of spirits, no state of recompense for what was done in the body; take that away and all religion falls to the ground. He adds a comparison of his own century — as there are men now who call themselves free-thinkers and are really false-thinkers, so there were Sadducees then, who bantered a doctrine plainly revealed in the Old Testament and held as an article of the Jewish faith.

The law they cite is real, and Ambrose reads it strictly before turning it. By the letter a woman is compelled to marry, however unwilling, so that a brother may raise up seed to his dead brother; the letter therefore kills, while the Spirit is the master of charity. Theophylact explains why the sect could build anything at all on it: imagining that life after the resurrection would be carnal, they were justly misled, and having decided the doctrine was impossible they invented a story to ridicule it. Bede calls the story what it is — a base fable devised to convict of folly those who assert the resurrection — and traces the whole error to reading the scriptures without understanding them.

Henry describes the method rather than the men. It is common practice, when someone means to undermine a truth of God, to perplex it and load it with difficulties; so here a question is raised on the supposition of the doctrine, framed so that no answer either way would satisfy. And the question is idle on its own terms: whose wife she was is not material at all, since death ends that relation and it is not to be resumed.

Two allegorical readings are offered, and they pull in different directions. Ambrose makes the woman the synagogue with her seven husbands, set against the Samaritan woman with five — the Samaritan following only the five books of Moses, the synagogue for the most part seven — and from none of them has she received the seed of an inheritance, so that she can have no part with her husbands in the resurrection, having turned a spiritual precept into a carnal one. The brother meant, on his reading, is not any brother in the flesh but the one who from the dead people of the Jews should claim the wisdom of divine worship for a wife and raise seed from it in the Apostles, left as it were unformed in the synagogue's womb and preserved by the admixture of a new seed. Bede's reading is bleaker: the seven brothers answer to the reprobate, fruitless in good works through the whole life of a world that revolves in seven days, carried off one after another until the course of the evil age passes away like the barren woman herself.
34:
The answer refuses the premise rather than the arithmetic. Theophylact says the point is that there will be no fleshly manner of life in the resurrection at all, which pulls down the doctrine along with the slender foundation it stood on. Augustine gives the reasoning in one chain: marriages exist for children, children for succession, succession because of death — so where there is no death there are no marriages. Clarke and Wesley both put the same thing from the side of this world, procreation being needed to repair the waste death makes and keep the species going.

Ellicott notes that the contrast of the two ages is Luke's own. The other Gospels do not set the children of this age against the children of that age, and no other New Testament writer uses that phrase for the life of the eternal kingdom, where the common expression is the world to come; both terms rest on time rather than place. He observes too that the verb for being accounted worthy is shared only by Luke and Paul, and Gill is careful about how a man comes to be so accounted — not by his own works or merit but through the blood and righteousness of the Messiah.

The reason given for the change is mortality's end, and Ellicott draws out what it implies: death and marriage are correlative facts in the government of the world, the one filling the gaps the other makes, so that where no gaps are made none need filling. Robertson notes that the word for equal to the angels is rare, late, and found nowhere else in the New Testament, Mark and Matthew having only as angels. Cyril supplies the ground of the comparison — the angels are a very great multitude and yet not propagated by generation, having their being from creation, so that those who rise have no more need of marriage than they. Theophylact explains the second title from the first: since it is God who works the resurrection, those regenerated by it are rightly called sons of God, there being nothing carnal in that regeneration, no coming together, no womb, no birth. Bede fills in what the state is like — made new by the glory of the resurrection, with no fear of death, no spot of corruption, no quality of an earthly condition, rejoicing in the perpetual sight of God's presence — and Augustine reaches for the same thing by a grammatical image: our speech is built of syllables that pass and follow one another, but the Word we shall then enjoy has all it has at once and everlastingly, and those who share it neither depart by death nor succeed by birth.

Bede enters one caution against reading the promise too narrowly. It must not be taken as if only the worthy will rise, or only they be without marriage; sinners rise too, and are without marriage in that new world. Our Lord named the elect alone in order to draw his hearers to search into the glory of the resurrection.
37:
The proof text is chosen with an eye to the audience. Bede and Calvin both note that the Sadducees received only the five books, so that the more obvious testimonies from the prophets would have carried no weight; Calvin adds that they had themselves brought Moses forward, and that Christ answered from the same writer deliberately. The argument turns on a tense. Theophylact puts it plainly: had the patriarchs gone to nothing, God would have said I was, as we say of a thing dead and gone that we were once its master; saying I am, he shows himself the God of the living. Calvin locates the force elsewhere — not in the idiom but in the promise, since God offers himself as our God only on condition of taking us for his people, and no man can be a father without children or a king without a people. Wesley states the same in a line, that it cannot properly be said God is the God of any who have utterly perished.

Two further notes are added. Bede sees the sequence of the proof: having established that souls survive death, which the Sadducees denied, Christ can then bring in the resurrection of the bodies which shared in the good or evil done — and meanwhile the just live truly to God even while dead in the body. Chrysostom takes the divine name itself as an affection rather than a limitation. God does not so delight in being called the God of heaven and earth as the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob; naming these does not narrow his dominion but enlarges it, since his power is shown less by the multitude of his subjects than by the virtue of his servants — and where men name a servant from his master, here the master takes his name from the servant.

That the argument was not novel to Jewish ears is worth recording, and two witnesses record it. Lightfoot and Clarke both quote the rabbinic story in which Moses, told to find ten righteous men and able to name only seven, asks whether the dead live, and on being answered yes replies at once, then remember Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Clarke sets beside it a sentence from the account of the Maccabees — that those who lose their lives for the sake of God live unto God, as do Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and the rest of the patriarchs — and concludes that neither the resurrection of the dead nor the survival of the soul was a strange doctrine among the Jews.
39:
The commendation comes from the wrong quarter, and every witness notices it. Robertson identifies the speakers as Pharisees, delighted to see the Pentateuch itself turned against the Sadducees, and points out the oddity flatly — they praise the reply though they remain hostile to the man who gave it. Ellicott softens that slightly, taking the words for the better sort of Pharisee, glad of a new defence of the doctrine their faith rested on. Gill says simply that these were scribes who believed the resurrection, and so were pleased with the reasoning.

Calvin will not credit them with more than the words. He supposes their good dispositions doubtful and the confession extorted by a secret exercise of divine power: they might have preferred to see Christ disgracefully silenced, but once his answer had fortified them against the rival sect, ambition led them to congratulate him — or perhaps envy, since they could not bear that the Sadducees should be the ones to carry a victory over him. What was really at work, Calvin thinks, was the providence that brought his deadliest enemies to assent to his doctrine. He adds one melancholy observation about the state of religion at the time: it counted as a wonder that the hope of the resurrection could be proved so ably out of the Law.

Henry uses the same testimony as evidence about the witnesses rather than the answer. Christ had the word of his adversaries that he had said well — men who opposed him because he would not conform to the traditions of the elders, but who could still recognise a defence of the fundamentals of religion when they heard one. Many who call themselves Christians, he adds, come short even of that.

The silence that follows is measured carefully. Robertson notes the double negative and the imperfect tense, and says the courage of Pharisees, Sadducees and Herodians alike had simply vanished; Clarke reads it as a decision not to venture another question for fear of being confounded again. Henry sets the fear beside its opposite — the disciples, weak as they were, dared ask him anything, being willing to receive his teaching, while those who cavilled at it dared ask nothing. Wesley enters a small correction to any absolute reading: the Sadducees dared not, but one of the scribes did, immediately afterwards.

Ellicott raises the question that silence leaves open. Luke omits the exchange about the great commandment which Matthew and Mark both record here, and which would have suited his Gospel's temper particularly well. He can offer no account of the omission except that Luke may not have known of it — and takes it, whatever the cause, as one more proof of how independent a narrator Luke is.
41:
Having been asked questions all morning, he asks one, and Theophylact marks the manner of it. With the passion close at hand he proclaims his own Godhead, and does it neither incautiously nor boastfully but with modesty — putting a question, throwing them into perplexity, and leaving them to draw the conclusion. Robertson identifies whose opinion is being quoted: the Pharisees are still gathered, and it is the rabbis' own formula that Jesus turns against them.

Ambrose is careful about what is and is not being criticised. They are not blamed for calling him David's son — the blind man was healed for saying it and the children were praised for crying Hosanna to the Son of David — but for not believing him also to be the Son of God. From the quoted verse he draws the doctrine directly: both the Father is Lord and the Son is Lord, yet there are not two Lords but one, the Father being in the Son and the Son in the Father. Sitting at the right hand neither honours him with something he lacked nor degrades him by the sending, for degrees of dignity are not looked for where the fullness of divinity is. And the subjection of enemies proves agreement rather than opposition, since the Father puts down the Son's enemies while the Son glorifies the Father on earth — the one working in the other by unity of nature, not by any weakness of power.

Augustine warns against taking the posture literally. We are not to imagine limbs, with the Father seated on the left and the Son on the right; the right hand is itself the power received by that Man who was taken up into God, so that he who came first to be judged should come to judge. Cyril reads the seat as a proof of heavenly glory — equal throne, equal majesty — and adds that sitting, said of God, signifies universal kingdom and power: the Word proceeding from the Father's substance does not put off his divine glory by being made flesh. Clarke takes the footstool at its full weight, the enemies not merely humbled enough for a foot to rest on them but wholly subjected to the Christ they were then about to crucify.

Chrysostom compresses the puzzle into a sentence: David was both the father and the servant of Christ, the one according to the flesh, the other in the Spirit. Henry states it as the plain contradiction it looked like — if the Messiah is David's son, why does David call him Lord; if he is David's Lord, why do we call him son — and gives the resolution the scribes could not: as God he was David's Lord, as man David's son, at once the root and the offspring of David. Robertson makes the same point about the psalm's two natures and observes that these are precisely the problems which troubled the rabbis then and trouble critics still. Cyril turns the argument forward to a later controversy, putting the same question to those who will not confess the Son of the holy Virgin to be true God, and so divide one Son into two: how is David's son David's Lord, and that not by any human lordship but a divine one?

Lightfoot supplies the historical footnote. Matthew records that no man was able to answer a word, and Lightfoot observes that the evasions later used had plainly not yet been invented — the Talmudists applying the psalm to Abraham, the Targum apparently to David, and others, as Justin Martyr complains to Trypho, to Hezekiah. Robertson notes what the wording assumes about authorship, that Jesus treats David as the writer of the psalm, and leaves the modern dispute standing beside the natural sense of the words.
45:
The warning is public, and the timing is deliberate. Robertson renders the construction as a genitive absolute — while all the people were listening — and remarks that this is the moment to speak; Gill says the words were spoken for the people's sake as much as the disciples'. Chrysostom explains why the moment had come. Nothing is more powerful than argument from the prophets, which carries more weight even than miracles: when Christ worked wonders he was often contradicted, but when he cited the prophets men fell silent, having nothing to say — and it is into that silence that the warning is spoken. Theophylact adds the reason it is addressed to disciples: they were being sent to teach the world, and must not imitate the pride they had just watched.

Cyril names the two faults exactly — the love of vainglory and the love of gain — and the details are sorted between them. The long robes belong to the first, and Lightfoot documents them from the rabbis: the inner garment of a disciple of the wise reaching to the sole of the foot, the outer one cut so that the inner should not show below it by more than a handbreadth. The greetings in the markets belong there too, or, as Theophylact allows, to the second, being the way of men who hunt a reputation or else use it to collect money.

On the chief seats Bede enters a distinction worth keeping. He does not forbid sitting first in the synagogue or at a feast to those whose place it rightly is; what is denounced is the love of the distinction, not the distinction. Though he adds that the other is not blameless either, when the same men who want to be in the disputes of the market also want to be called masters in the synagogue. And he gives two reasons why we are told to beware of such men rather than merely to disapprove of them: lest we be led away by their appearance, taking what they do for good, or else be inflamed with jealousy and want the praise they get for deeds they only pretend to.

The second fault is the graver, and the language about it is unsparing. Bede describes the mechanism: passing for righteous and of great merit with God, they take large sums from the sick and from people whose consciences are troubled, as men who will be their protectors at the judgment. Chrysostom presses the image in the word — they thrust themselves into widows' possessions and grind down their poverty, not content to eat what is offered but devouring — and adds that turning prayer to such an end is what exposes them to the heavier sentence. Theophylact puts the aggravation plainly: they do not merely do evil but make a show of prayer, using virtue as the cover for the sin, and they impoverish the very widows they were bound to pity, their visits alone driving them to great expense. Gill sets the two verses against each other as a pair, the one exposing their pride and the other their avarice.

Clarke closes on what the warning costs. A bad example supported by the authority and reputation and majesty of religion is a very subtle poison, and it is a great misfortune for a people to have to beware of the very persons who ought to be their rule and pattern. He refuses to let the point be used by one party against another: such ministers are found in the branches as well as in the root, among the separated bodies as much as in the churches they left, and on neither hand is there room for glorying.
